summary: NISAR Time Machine is a free web app that shows anyone how the land changed after a wildfire, using the NASA–ISRO NISAR radar. Radar sees through smoke, cloud and darkness, but its images are hard to read, and two dates can only be compared fairly if the satellite looked from the same orbit. Our app does that work for the user. Pick a fire from NASA's EONET list or any place on the globe: the app finds NISAR passes from the same orbit, puts them on a timeline and shows before, during and after side by side. Every result is explained in one plain sentence, together with how confident it is, and users can draw an area to see how many hectares changed. In Spain, the radar signal dropped over 2,118 ha of burned land. In Muğla, Türkiye, it dropped over only about 9 ha, while 6,534 ha were reported burned; our hypothesis is that the burned trunks are still standing. The app needs no account and no install, and all processing code is open. We built it so that people who live near a fire, not only experts, can see for themselves what happened to their forest.
details:
Live app: https://serhanensar.github.io/GevrekOverFlow-SpaceApps2026/

Code: https://github.com/SerhanEnsar/GevrekOverFlow-SpaceApps2026

What it does

NISAR Time Machine turns NISAR L-band radar into a story anyone can read. A 3D globe shows where NISAR is right now and where it has looked. A fires panel lists recent wildfires from NASA EONET; clicking one opens the time machine for that place. The time machine picks up to six NISAR passes from the same orbit track, so every date is seen from the same angle, and plays them before, during and after the event. Each result comes with a plain-language sentence ("the forest signal dropped here") and a confidence level. Users can draw a rectangle, circle or polygon anywhere and get the area of change in hectares. A story mode and a "Reading the colours" guide explain what the radar colours mean, so no prior SAR knowledge is needed.

How it works

We read NISAR Level-2 GCOV products (HH and HV backscatter). A Python pipeline finds scenes through NASA CMR and ASF, keeps only passes that cover at least 90% of the area, groups them by orbit geometry parsed from the file name, removes single-polarisation passes, reduces speckle with a 3x3 filter in linear power and regrids everything to a common grid. Simple, published rules classify each pixel (water, forest, shrub, open land), and a change of 3 dB or more between comparable dates marks real change. Confidence comes from shifting every threshold by ±0.5 dB and checking whether the answer stays the same. For any place outside our prepared showcases, the browser reads NISAR imagery from NASA GIBS and converts colours back to decibels with a model we fitted and checked against the original files (about ±1 dB error, 85% class agreement).

Findings

Spain: the cross-polarised (HV) signal dropped from about -15 dB to about -20 dB over 2,118 ha of burned forest, while an unburned control area stayed near -15 dB. Muğla, Türkiye: only about 9 ha dropped, while 6,534 ha were reported burned. Our hypothesis is that burned trunks are still standing and keep reflecting the radar. We present this as an open question, not a result.

Benefits and intended impact

Radar sees through smoke and cloud and works at night, exactly when wildfire areas are hardest to see. Today, using NISAR data needs downloads, specialist software and knowledge of orbit geometry. Our app removes those steps: no account, no install, works in any browser. People who live near a burned area, local authorities, teachers and journalists can check what changed and follow recovery every 12 days, and researchers can reuse the open pipeline.

Tools and languages

Python (asf_search, h5py, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, shapely, Pillow, requests) for the pipeline; JavaScript with MapLibre GL JS, satellite.js and Chart.js for the web app; GitHub Pages for hosting. No special hardware.

What makes it creative

Instead of showing radar as an unexplained image, the app tells the user what changed, where and how sure it is. It compares only dates that are really comparable, and it treats a surprising result (Muğla) as a question worth asking.

What we considered

Honesty: every number on the site is reproducible from the code, and limits are stated on the page (the global layer is experimental, single-pol passes are excluded, GIBS colours are an approximation). Accessibility: plain language, no login, works on a laptop. Openness: only open NASA data and open-source libraries.

Use of AI tools

We used an AI assistant (a large language model) for coding help and debugging, literature search, checking our analysis and English editing. The idea, design decisions, data choices and the validation of every number are our own.
